author: ValWood
body:
CRYM is annotated to 


UniProtKB:Q14894 | CRYM | involved_in | GO:0070327    thyroid hormone transport
from PMID:11897713

However, that idea wasn't widely confirmed. Later work,
reviewed in  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9202446/
does not support this conclusion, and  it seems that it rather sequesters thyroid hormone in the cytosol

This 2022 review summarizes 2 roles:

1. Thyroid hormone storage. The current view is that CRYM may play a key role in intracellular sequestration and storage of thyroid hormone. It holds T3 inside cells rather than shuttling it to mitochondria, as the 1986 paper proposed. 
2.  It also acts as a ketimine reductase in the lysine degradation pathway when it is not bound to thyroid hormone. It belongs to the ornithine cyclodeaminase/mu-crystallin family, with sequence similarity to bacterial ornithine cyclodeaminases. T3 binding switches the reductase off,  linking thyroid status to amino acid metabolism. 

I'll raise a dispute for the "GO:0070327    thyroid hormone transport"
pointing to this ticket, but I haven't dug into the  sequestering activity, I'll try to find better supporting evidence other than this review which  isn't ecplicit, before I open the  disputes.

As expected from the high levels of Crym expressed in the muscles of the transgenic mice, we observed a large accumulation of intracellular T3 (~190-fold) in the TA muscle compared to controls. μ-Crystallin promotes accumulation of T3 in the cytoplasm in part by sequestering the hormone.
